reason: The sources support over 10 cross-verified claims detailing the long-term fate of Earth's continents, oceans, and eventual solar destruction.
story: Long before the Sun dies, Earth will face dramatic transformations. Driven by mantle convection, tectonic plates moving a few centimeters per year will merge the continents into a new supercontinent in a repeating cycle every few hundred million years. In about 50 million years, Africa will smash into Europe, closing the Mediterranean Sea and raising massive mountains. Geologists predict future supercontinents like Amasia or Pangaea Proxima, where extreme climates and violent monsoons dominate. But Earth's ultimate fate rests with the Sun. In about five billion years, our star will exhaust its core hydrogen fuel and balloon into a red giant. While inner worlds like Mercury and Venus are swallowed, gas giants Jupiter and Saturn could survive, continuing to orbit the dense white dwarf remnant left behind after the Sun's outer layers blow away.
angle: When the Sun exhausts its fuel in five billion years and turns into a red giant, outer gas giants like Jupiter and Saturn could survive while inner planets are destroyed, eventually orbiting a tiny white dwarf.

claims.claim: Tectonic plates move across Earth's surface at a rate of a few centimeters, or about 15 millimeters, per year.
Continental drift and plate movements are driven by heat circulation and mantle convection within Earth.
Subduction occurs where tectonic plates meet and one plate is pulled or forced beneath another into the mantle.
Earth's continents periodically collide to form a single supercontinent every 400 to 700 million years.
In about 50 million years, Africa's northward shift will close the Mediterranean Sea and build a massive mountain range in southern Europe.
Geologist Paul Hoffman proposed the future supercontinent Amasia, formed by North and South America advancing across the Pacific to merge with Asia.
Geologist Christopher Scotese proposed a future supercontinent initially named Pangaea Ultima and later renamed Pangaea Proxima.
Asteroid or comet collisions present a recurring threat of mass extinction for life on Earth.
Supercontinents experience severe climate extremes, including intense heat, dry inland deserts, and violent monsoons.
In about five billion years, the Sun will exhaust the hydrogen fuel in its core.
After exhausting its core fuel, the Sun will expand into a massive red giant star.
The expanding red giant Sun is expected to overwhelm or swallow inner planets such as Mercury and Venus.
Outer gas giants like Jupiter and Saturn could survive the Sun's red giant phase.
After its red giant phase, the Sun will shrink into a hot, dense white dwarf star about half as massive as the Sun.

disputed: The exact duration of the supercontinent cycle varies across sources (400-500 million years versus 500-700 million years); scripts should refer broadly to 'every few hundred million years'.
The final arrangement of the next supercontinent is disputed between models like Amasia and Pangaea Proxima; scripts should frame these as competing geological predictions.
Whether Earth itself will be completely engulfed during the Sun's red giant phase is uncertain; scripts should note Earth's survival as an open question.
